verifications.claim: Colon cancer begins in the large intestine.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Colon cancer is a malignancy, abnormal cells, that begin in the colon or large intestine. (R2); Colorectal cancer is cancer that starts in the large intestine (colon) or the rectum (R4)
verifications.reasoning: Direct statements in multiple references confirm colon cancer originates in the large intestine (colon).

verifications.claim: Colon cancer typically starts as small, noncancerous polyps that grow over time.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Most colon and rectal cancers begin as benign (non-cancerous) polyps. These are flat or knob-like growths... some may become malignant (cancerous) over time. (R2); Nearly all colorectal cancers begin as noncancerous (benign) lumps (polyps) in the lining of the colon and rectum. These can slowly develop into cancer. (R4)
verifications.reasoning: References explicitly state most colon cancers start as benign polyps that can become cancerous over time.

verifications.claim: Colon cancer screening generally starts at age 45.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: For those who have no family history of the disease, recommended screenings begin at age 45 (R2); All adults age 45 and older should have a colon cancer screening. (R4)
verifications.reasoning: Multiple sources recommend screening starting at age 45 for average risk individuals.

verifications.claim: Many polyps do not produce symptoms.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Occasionally, the growths produce symptoms such as bleeding, constipation, or blood in the stool. Most often, however, the cells often produce no symptoms (R2)
verifications.reasoning: Directly states most polyps produce no symptoms.

verifications.claim: Many early-stage cancers do not produce symptoms.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Sometimes, No Symptoms at All Remember: Many people diagnosed with colorectal cancer report no symptoms. Regular screening is crucial (R1)
verifications.reasoning: Explicitly notes many colorectal cancers, especially early, have no symptoms.

verifications.claim: Colorectal cancer staging is determined by the TNM system.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Treatment decisions can be made with reference to the TNM (tumor, node, metastasis) classification (R6)
verifications.reasoning: References confirm TNM is the standard staging system for colorectal cancer.

verifications.claim: TNM stands for tumor, node, metastasis.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: TNM (tumor, node, metastasis) classification (R6)
verifications.reasoning: Direct definition provided.

verifications.claim: Stage 0 colorectal cancer is carcinoma in situ.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Stage 0: Cancer has not grown past the inner layer of the colon or rectum (carcinoma in situ). (R2)
verifications.reasoning: Exact match.

verifications.claim: Stage 0 colorectal cancer is localized to the inner lining.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Stage 0: Cancer has not grown past the inner layer of the colon or rectum (R2)
verifications.reasoning: Directly describes Stage 0 as confined to the inner layer.

verifications.claim: In Stage I and II colorectal cancer, the cancer has grown into the muscle layers of the colon wall.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Stage I: Cancer has grown past the inner layer... into other layers of the colon... Stage II: Cancer has grown into or through the outer layer of the colon wall (R2); Stage I: Cancer is in the inner layers of the colon. Stage II: Cancer has spread through the muscle wall of the colon (R4)
verifications.reasoning: Stages I and II involve growth into/through muscle layers, precisely matching.

verifications.claim: In Stage I and II colorectal cancer, the cancer has not spread outside the colon.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Stage I: ...but has not spread to the lymph nodes or nearby tissues. Stage II: ...but has not spread to nearby tissues or lymph nodes. (R2)
verifications.reasoning: Explicitly no spread outside colon for Stages I and II.

verifications.claim: In Stage III colorectal cancer, the cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Stage III: Cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes, but not to other organs. (R2)
verifications.reasoning: Direct definition.

verifications.claim: Stage IV colorectal cancer is metastatic cancer.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Stage IV: Cancer has spread to other organs beyond the colon (R2)
verifications.reasoning: Stage IV defined by distant spread, i.e., metastatic.

verifications.claim: In Stage IV colorectal cancer, the cancer has spread to distant organs like the liver or lungs.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Stage IV: Cancer has spread to other organs beyond the colon, such as the liver, lungs, or others. (R2)
verifications.reasoning: Exact examples match.

verifications.claim: Colon cancer risk increases particularly after age 45 or 50.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: People who are over the age of 45 also have a higher risk of forming polyps in the colon... recommended screenings begin at age 45 as this is when the risk of getting colon cancer begins to increase. (R2)
verifications.reasoning: Risk increase noted at 45, aligning with claim.

verifications.claim: Lynch syndrome is an inherited risk factor for colon cancer.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer syndrome (HNPCC, Lynch syndrome) poses about a 40% lifetime risk... HNPCC is a cause of about 6% of all colon cancers. (R3)
verifications.reasoning: Explicitly identified as inherited risk factor.

verifications.claim: Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is an inherited risk factor for colon cancer.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Hereditary mutation of the APC gene is the cause of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), in which affected individuals carry an almost 100% risk of developing colon cancer by age 40 years. (R3)
verifications.reasoning: Directly stated.

verifications.claim: High consumption of red/processed meats is a lifestyle risk factor for colon cancer.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Epidemiologic studies have linked increased risk of colorectal cancer with a diet high in red meat and animal fat... intake of proinflammatory diets (replete in red, processed... meat...) was associated with a significantly higher risk (R3)
verifications.reasoning: Explicit link to red/processed meats.

verifications.claim: Lack of exercise is a lifestyle risk factor for colon cancer.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Obesity and lifestyle choices such as... sedentary habits have also been associated with increased risk for colorectal cancer. (R3)
verifications.reasoning: Sedentary habits directly indicate lack of exercise.

verifications.claim: Obesity is a lifestyle risk factor for colon cancer.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Obesity and lifestyle choices such as cigarette smoking, alcohol consumption, and sedentary habits have also been associated with increased risk for colorectal cancer. (R3)
verifications.reasoning: Explicitly listed.

verifications.claim: Smoking is a lifestyle risk factor for colon cancer.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Obesity and lifestyle choices such as cigarette smoking... have also been associated with increased risk... A meta-analysis... found a modest but significant elevation of colorectal cancer risk in current smokers (R3)
verifications.reasoning: Direct association.

verifications.claim: Excessive alcohol use is a lifestyle risk factor for colon cancer.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Obesity and lifestyle choices such as cigarette smoking, alcohol consumption... have also been associated with increased risk... both lifetime and baseline alcohol consumption increase colorectal cancer risk. (R3)
verifications.reasoning: Explicitly stated.

verifications.claim: Colon cancer treatment includes surgery.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Surgery currently is the definitive treatment modality. (R3); Treatments may include: ... Surgery (R4); Standard treatment for patients with colon cancer has been open surgical resection (R6)
verifications.reasoning: Consistently identified as primary treatment.

verifications.claim: Colon cancer treatment includes chemotherapy.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Until the mid-1990s, the only approved agent... was 5-fluorouracil. Since then, new agents... Cytotoxic agents (eg, irinotecan, oxaliplatin) (R3); Treatments may include: ... Chemotherapy (R4)
verifications.reasoning: Standard treatment option.

verifications.claim: Colon cancer treatment includes targeted therapy.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Biologic agents (eg, bevacizumab, cetuximab, panitumumab, pembrolizumab, nivolumab) (R3); Targeted therapy (R6)
verifications.reasoning: Explicitly listed.

verifications.claim: Colon cancer treatment includes immunotherapy.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Biologic agents (eg, bevacizumab, cetuximab, panitumumab, pembrolizumab, nivolumab) (R3); Immunotherapy (R6)
verifications.reasoning: Pembrolizumab and nivolumab are immunotherapies.

verifications.claim: The 5-year survival rate for localized cancer is around 91%.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Localized disease: 91.1% (R3)
verifications.reasoning: Exact match for localized (Stage I) 5-year survival.

verifications.claim: The 5-year survival rate for cancer spread to distant parts of the body is around 15.7%.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Distant disease: 15.7% (R3)
verifications.reasoning: Precise figure for distant metastatic disease.

verifications.claim: Colon cancer symptoms include changes in bowel habits such as diarrhea, constipation, or narrowing of the stool lasting more than a few days.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Change in Bowel Habits Diarrhea... Constipation... A Thin, narrow, or ribbon-like stool... Contact your healthcare provider if it continues longer than three days... If your constipation lasts longer than two weeks (R1)
verifications.reasoning: Symptoms directly described with duration notes.

verifications.claim: Colon cancer symptoms include rectal bleeding such as bright red blood or very dark/black, tarry stool.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Blood in Your Stool or Bleeding from the Rectum... Blood in the toilet, on the stool... Color: Blood, darkened, or tarry (black) stool (R1)
verifications.reasoning: Exact symptom description.

verifications.claim: Colon cancer symptoms include abdominal discomfort such as persistent cramps, gas, pain, or a feeling that the bowel does not empty completely.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Persistent Cramps or Low Back Pain... Stomach discomfort or cramping that doesn’t go away... Feeling Bloated or an Urge to Have a Bowel Movement... even when there is no need to have one, could indicate changes in your colon preventing a complete bowel evacuation. (R1)
verifications.reasoning: Matches persistent cramps, gas, pain, incomplete emptying.

verifications.claim: Colon cancer symptoms include systemic changes such as unexplained weight loss, weakness, fatigue, or anemia.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Unexplained or Unintentional Weight Loss... Fatigue or Weakness... Anemia... Symptoms: ... fatigue and pale skin. (R1)
verifications.reasoning: All listed symptoms directly covered.

verifications.claim: Regular screenings such as colonoscopy allow for the identification and removal of polyps before they turn into cancer.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: The best way to detect the presence of polyps is with a procedure called a colonoscopy... when a physician finds polyps during a colonoscopy, they are generally removed during the procedure. (R2)
verifications.reasoning: Explicitly states colonoscopy identifies and removes polyps before malignancy.
